# File type filtering

The `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear` and `--type-list`
flags are all implemented by one module: `ignore::types`, in
`crates/ignore/src/types.rs`. The default definitions live beside it in
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. Everything else is wiring: ripgrep's
`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` turns flags into a matcher, and
`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs` consults it while walking.

## How a definition is represented

A definition is a `FileTypeDef`, which is a name and a list of glob strings:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }
```

`TypesBuilder` holds them in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` keyed by name.
`TypesBuilder::add(name, glob)` appends one glob to the entry for `name`,
creating it if it doesn't exist. It rejects the name `all`, which is reserved,
and any name containing a character that isn't alphanumeric, so `web2` is a
legal type name and `c++` or `my-type` are not. Note that `add` doesn't
deduplicate, so adding the same glob twice gives you the glob twice.

`TypesBuilder::add_def` parses the string form users type on the command line.
It splits on `:` and dispatches on the number of parts: two parts means
`{name}:{glob}`, and three parts means `{name}:include:{comma-separated names}`.
An include is resolved eagerly. It clones the globs of each named type and
re-adds them under the new name, after first checking that every name exists so
a partial definition can't be left behind. That means an include is a snapshot,
not a reference. Definitions added to `wat` after `combo:include:wat` won't
appear in `combo`. Because the parse splits on `:`, a glob containing a colon
can't be expressed this way.

`add_defaults` walks `DEFAULT_TYPES`, a `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` of alias lists
paired with glob lists. Each name in the first slice gets every glob in the
second, so `(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])` produces two independent
definitions with identical globs.

## Selections and how the matcher is built

Definitions on their own filter nothing. `select` and `negate` push a
`Selection<()>` onto an ordered `Vec`, and that order is the flag order.
Passing the name `all` to either one expands to a selection per currently
defined type, iterating `HashMap` keys, so the relative order within one `all`
is unspecified. Only the position of the `all` group as a whole is meaningful.

`TypesBuilder::build` walks the selections in order and does three things at
once. It looks up each selection's `FileTypeDef`, returning
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if the name was never defined or was removed by
`clear`. It compiles every glob of that definition with
`GlobBuilder::literal_separator(true)` into a shared `GlobSetBuilder`. And it
pushes `(selection index, glob index)` onto `glob_to_selection`, giving a map
from a position in the flat `GlobSet` back to the selection that contributed it.
`build` also records `has_selected`, true when at least one selection isn't a
negation, and stores `defs`, the full sorted list of definitions, which is what
`--type-list` prints from `main.rs`.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob>`. Read it in order:

- Directories always return `Match::None`. File types never prune a directory,
  so selecting a type doesn't reduce how much of the tree ripgrep walks.
- Matching runs against the file name only, via `pathutil::file_name`. A
  definition whose glob contains a path separator can't match anything.
- `GlobSet::matches_into` fills a scratch `Vec<usize>` with the indices of every
  matching glob, sorted ascending and deduplicated. `matched` takes the last
  one, which is therefore the glob from the latest selection, and that's the
  precedence rule: the last matching `-t` or `-T` on the command line wins.
- The winning selection decides the result. A negation yields `Match::Ignore`, a
  selection yields `Match::Whitelist`, and both carry a `Glob` reporting the
  responsible `FileTypeDef`.
- If nothing matched and `has_selected` is true, the path becomes
  `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())`, whose `file_type_def()` is `None`. This is
  what makes `-trust` exclude everything that isn't Rust. With only negations,
  an unmatched path is `Match::None`.

The scratch vector comes from an `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`, so `matched` takes
`&self`, `Types` is cheap to clone, and parallel walkers each get their own
buffer.

`Ignore::matched` in `dir.rs` calls this last, after `overrides` and after the
gitignore-style matchers, and only when `Types::is_empty()` is false. That
ordering is the documented precedence: `-g` beats ignore files, which beat
`-t`.

## Changing this area

Adding a default type means one tuple in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, kept sorted by the
first alias (`default_types_are_sorted` asserts it), wrapped to 79 columns, and
under `#[rustfmt::skip]`. Prefer globs that stay in the fast `GlobSet`
strategies: a plain extension or a literal file name is cheaper than a pattern
that falls through to the regex strategy.

If you touch precedence or the empty-match rules, the unit tests at the bottom
of `types.rs` cover them through the `matched!` macro, and `tests/misc.rs`
covers the flags end to end (`file_types`, `file_types_negate_all`,
`file_type_clear`, `file_type_add_compose`). `--type-clear rust -t rust` is
expected to fail at build time with a non-empty stderr, not to silently match
nothing.
